title: Shkmeruli: Georgian Skillet Chicken in Garlic Milk
blurb: Chicken pressed flat until the skin shatters, then drowned in a hot milk sauce loaded with a truly reckless amount of grated garlic and blue-fenugreek warmth.

steps.text: Pat the thighs bone-dry with paper towels and season both sides hard with salt and pepper. Press each one flat with the heel of your hand so it will sit in full contact with the pan.
steps.tip: Any surface moisture steams the skin instead of crisping it.

steps.text: Set a cast iron skillet over medium heat and lay the thighs in skin side down, then set a smaller heavy pan directly on top to weigh them down. Cook without moving them until the fat has rendered out and the skin is deep amber and lacquer-crisp.
steps.tip: The weight is what gives shkmeruli its signature flat, crackling skin.

steps.text: Lift off the weight, flip the thighs, and cook the second side until the meat is firm and the juices run clear at the bone. Move the chicken to a plate skin side up while you build the sauce.

Pour off all but about 1 tbsp of the fat and drop the heat to low. Melt the butter in, then add the grated garlic and stir constantly until it smells sweet and looks pale gold but has taken on no color at all.
steps.tip: Browned garlic turns bitter and ruins the sauce.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander, fenugreek, paprika, and cayenne and let them bloom in the butter for a few seconds until fragrant. Pour in the milk and cream, scraping the bottom of the pan clean.
steps.tip: Fenugreek is the flavor that makes this taste Georgian rather than French.

steps.text: Raise the heat to medium-low and simmer the sauce, stirring often, until it thickens enough to leave a clear trail behind your spoon and turns pale ivory. Season it aggressively with salt and taste for garlic bite.
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy blip; a hard boil will curdle the milk.

steps.text: Nestle the thighs back in skin side up so the sauce comes only halfway up the sides, keeping that crisp skin above the waterline. Spoon sauce over the meat and let it warm through.
steps.tip: Never submerge the skin you worked so hard for.

steps.text: Warm the naan directly over a burner or in a dry pan until blistered and pliable. Shower the chicken with cilantro and serve straight from the skillet with the bread for mopping.
steps.tip: The sauce is the point; the bread is the delivery system.

swap: No fenugreek in the cupboard? Use 1 tsp curry powder plus an extra 1/2 tsp coriander for a similar savory-sweet hum.
leftovers: Refrigerate up to 3 days and reheat gently in a covered skillet over low with a splash of milk; the sauce tightens and the skin softens, so shred the meat into the sauce and eat it over rice.

title: Nigerian Suya Steak with Yaji and Raw Onion
blurb: Thin ribbons of beef blitzed under the broiler and buried in yaji, the peanut-and-chili suya spice that clings like dust and hits smoky, nutty, and genuinely hot.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb beef sirloin or flank steak
1/2 cup Southern Grove roasted unsalted peanuts
1 large red onion, sliced paper thin

steps.text: Put the steak on a plate in the freezer to firm up so it slices cleanly. While it chills, drop the peanuts into a food processor or a zip bag and pulse or crush them to a coarse, sandy powder.
steps.tip: Stop before it turns to paste; the oil should stay locked in the crumbs.

steps.text: Stir the peanut powder together with the smoked paprika, cayenne, ginger, onion powder, garlic powder, crushed bouillon, and 1 tsp salt. Split this yaji into two piles and set half aside for finishing.
steps.tip: Half the yaji cooks on, half goes on raw for punch.

steps.text: Slice the chilled steak against the grain into strips about a quarter inch thick. Toss them with the oil, then rub in the first pile of yaji until every strip is coated and slightly damp.
steps.tip: Slicing against the grain is what keeps thin beef tender.

steps.text: Move an oven rack to the top slot and heat the broiler to high. Thread the strips onto skewers in loose ripples, or just spread them in a single layer on a foil-lined sheet with space between the pieces.
steps.tip: Crowding steams the beef and you lose the char.

steps.text: Broil until the edges blacken in spots and the spice crust looks dry and toasted, then flip and broil the second side until just done. While it cooks, drop the sliced onion into ice water so it turns crisp and loses its harsh edge.
steps.tip: Suya is meant to be well-charred outside, blushing inside.

steps.text: Flip the skewers and finish the second side under the broiler, watching closely since the peanut in the rub can go from toasted to burnt fast.
Let the beef rest on the pan so the juices settle, then drain the onion and pat it dry. Shower the hot steak with most of the reserved yaji so it sticks to the surface.
steps.tip: Raw yaji on hot meat is the whole trick.

steps.text: Pile the steak on a platter with the cold onion and tomato slices scattered over the top. Serve with lime wedges and the last of the yaji in a dish for dredging bite by bite.
steps.tip: Eat it with your hands, standing up, the way it is sold on the street.

swap: No sirloin? Thin-sliced Never Any! chicken thighs take the same rub beautifully; broil them a couple of minutes longer per side.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; slice cold and stuff into warm pita or protein wraps with more raw onion rather than reheating, which dulls the crust.

title: Basque Cod al Pil-Pil with Guindilla Chiles
blurb: Cod poached gently in a lake of olive oil, then swirled into a glossy pale-gold emulsion that comes from nothing but fish, garlic, and patience.

ingredients.item: 2 thick-cut cod loin pieces (about 1 lb total)
2 dried arbol or guindilla chiles, sliced into rings
3/4 cup Specially Selected extra virgin olive oil
1 cup jarred piquillo or roasted red peppers, torn

steps.text: Salt the cod generously on all sides and set it on a rack or plate to sit at room temperature. Pat it completely dry before cooking, wiping away any beads of moisture the salt has pulled out.
steps.tip: Salting first firms the flesh and coaxes out the gelatin the sauce depends on.

steps.text: Pour the olive oil into a wide skillet or shallow casserole and add the garlic and chile rings. Set it over the lowest heat you can manage and let the garlic swim until it turns pale straw gold and the oil smells sweet.
steps.tip: If the garlic sizzles hard, the heat is too high; you want faint lazy bubbles.

steps.text: Scoop out the garlic and chiles with a slotted spoon and reserve them. Slide the cod into the warm oil skinned side down, making sure the oil comes at least halfway up each piece.
steps.tip: The oil should feel warm, not hot, when the fish goes in.

steps.text: Poach the fish over low heat, spooning oil over the top now and then, until the sides turn opaque white and small pearly bubbles gather around the edges. Flip carefully with a spatula and finish the second side until the flesh just begins to separate into flakes.
steps.tip: Those bubbles are the gelatin releasing; that is your sauce forming.

steps.text: Lift the cod out onto a warm plate and pull the pan off the heat. Let the oil cool for a couple of minutes so it stops shimmering, since a scorching pan will never emulsify.
steps.tip: Cooler oil emulsifies; hot oil splits.

steps.text: Tilt the pan and swirl it in steady circles, or work a fine sieve through the oil in small circles, until the clear oil clouds and thickens into a creamy, pale sauce the texture of loose mayonnaise. Keep going past the point where you think nothing is happening.
steps.tip: It turns all at once; sudden thickening means you did it right.

steps.text: Slide the cod back into the sauce along with any juices from the plate and warm it through over the lowest heat, tilting the pan to coat. Taste the sauce and correct with salt and a squeeze of lemon.

Tear the bread into thick slabs and griddle them in a spoonful of the garlicky oil until crisp at the edges. Plate the cod with the torn piquillos, scatter the reserved garlic chips, chiles, and parsley over the top, and serve the bread alongside.
steps.tip: Nobody leaves pil-pil sauce in the pan.

swap: Frozen cod works perfectly here; thaw it fully overnight and press it dry between towels, or use thick haddock or hake loins instead.
leftovers: Best the day it is made, but the fish and sauce keep 2 days refrigerated; rewarm very gently over low heat and re-swirl the pan to bring the emulsion back.

title: Hungarian Beef Goulash with Caraway and Sweet Paprika
blurb: A deep brick-red pot of beef gone spoon-tender in a paprika-saturated onion gravy, sharpened with caraway and finished with a cool swirl of sour cream.

ingredients.item: 3 lb beef chuck roast, cut in 1 1/2-inch cubes
2 red bell peppers, sliced in wide strips
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut in large chunks

steps.text: Pat the beef cubes very dry and season them all over with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until it just smokes, then brown the beef in two or three uncrowded batches until every piece has a dark crust on at least two sides.
steps.tip: Crowded meat sweats grey instead of browning.

steps.text: Move the beef to a bowl and drop the heat to medium. Add the onions with a big pinch of salt and cook, scraping the fond off the bottom as they release their water, until they collapse into a soft golden mass.
steps.tip: Goulash is really an onion sauce; do not rush this.

steps.text: Pull the pot completely off the heat and let it lose its sizzle for a moment. Stir in both paprikas, the caraway, and the tomato paste so the residual heat blooms them into a thick red paste that coats the onions.
steps.tip: Paprika scorches in seconds over direct heat and turns acrid.

steps.text: Return the pot to medium, pour in the broth and vinegar, and add the bay leaves. Slide the beef and every drop of its resting juices back in, then season with 2 tsp salt.

Bring it to a bare simmer where only a few bubbles break the surface, cover, and let it go low and slow, stirring once or twice. The beef should be nearly tender but still holding its shape when you check.
steps.tip: A rolling boil makes chuck stringy; keep it barely trembling.

steps.text: Add the potatoes and bell peppers, pushing them under the surface, and simmer uncovered so the gravy reduces. It is done when a knife slides into the beef with no resistance and the sauce coats the back of a spoon in a glossy red sheet.
steps.tip: A few potatoes breaking down is a good thing; it thickens the pot.

steps.text: Fish out the bay leaves, then taste and adjust with salt and another splash of vinegar if it tastes flat. Let the pot sit off the heat so the fat rises and the flavors settle.
steps.tip: Skim the surface fat if you want a cleaner-tasting gravy.

steps.text: Ladle into deep bowls and finish each with a spoonful of sour cream and a last pinch of sweet paprika. Stir the cream in at the table rather than into the pot.
steps.tip: Sour cream added to the whole pot can split on reheating.

swap: No chuck roast? Use 3 lb beef stew meat, or bone-in short ribs with the covered simmer stretched by 10 minutes.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months; it is noticeably better on day two, so reheat gently over low heat and thin with a splash of broth.

title: Yucatecan Sopa de Lima with Crisp Tortilla Strips
blurb: A clear, allspice-scented chicken broth blasted with charred lime and habanero, poured over a nest of tortilla strips fried crisp enough to crackle.

ingredients.item: 6 Casa Mamita corn tortillas, cut in thin strips

steps.text: Season the thighs on both sides with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high and sear the chicken until the undersides are golden brown, then flip once and pull the pan back to medium.
steps.tip: The browned bits on the bottom give this clear broth its backbone.

steps.text: Push the chicken aside, add the onion and tomatoes with a pinch of salt, and cook until the onion turns translucent and the tomatoes slump into the pan juices.
Stir in the oregano, allspice, and cumin and let them toast until you can smell the allspice clearly. Pour in the broth, add the halved habanero, and bring it to a gentle simmer.
steps.tip: Allspice is the signature note of Yucatecan cooking; do not skip it.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered, skimming any foam, until the chicken is cooked through and shreds easily against the side of the pot with a fork.
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy bubble so the broth stays clear rather than cloudy.

steps.text: While the soup simmers, heat the remaining oil in a skillet over medium-high and fry the tortilla strips in two batches, turning them, until they are stiff and pale gold. Drain them on paper towels and salt them right away.
steps.tip: Pull them a shade before they look done; they darken as they cool.

steps.text: Halve two of the limes and press them cut side down in a dry hot skillet until the surfaces are blackened and the juice inside is hot. Cut the remaining limes into wedges.
steps.tip: Charring pushes the lime from sour to smoky and slightly sweet.

steps.text: Pull the chicken out, shred it in big pieces, and return it to the pot. Fish out the habanero, then kill the heat and squeeze in the juice of the charred limes, tasting as you go until the broth is bracingly sour.
steps.tip: Add the lime off heat so it stays bright instead of turning bitter.

steps.text: Pile a handful of tortilla strips in the bottom of each bowl and ladle the hot soup over them. Finish with cilantro, extra strips on top, and lime wedges for squeezing at the table.
steps.tip: Serve immediately, while the strips still crunch.

swap: No corn tortillas? Fry strips of Casa Mamita flour tortillas or crush in a handful of plain tortilla chips just before serving.
leftovers: Refrigerate the broth and chicken up to 3 days, always storing the fried strips separately at room temperature; reheat the soup and add fresh lime juice each time.

title: Okinawan Pork and Tofu Champuru
blurb: A blistering-hot stir-fry of crisped pork belly, golden torn tofu, and charred cabbage bound with soft egg and finished with a snowdrift of dancing bonito flakes.

ingredients.item: 12 oz pork belly or thick-cut Appleton Farms bacon, cut in 1-inch strips
1/2 head green cabbage, cut in rough 2-inch squares
1 tsp Trader Joe's Mushroom & Company Multipurpose Umami Seasoning Blend
2 packages Trader Joe's Frozen Jasmine Rice

steps.text: Wrap the tofu block in a clean towel, set a heavy pan on top, and let it press while you prep everything else. Tear it into rough bite-size chunks rather than cubing it so the craggy edges catch color.
steps.tip: Torn tofu has more surface area and browns far better than neat cubes.

steps.text: Lay the pork strips in a cold wok or large skillet and set it over medium heat so the fat renders slowly. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the strips are deep brown and crisp at the edges and the pan holds a good slick of fat.
steps.tip: Starting cold renders more fat, which is the cooking medium for everything else.

steps.text: Scoop the pork onto a plate and leave the fat behind. Raise the heat to medium-high and add the tofu chunks in one layer, letting them sit undisturbed until a golden crust forms before turning them.
steps.tip: If you stir too soon the tofu shreds; wait for the release.

steps.text: Push the tofu to one side, beat the eggs with a pinch of salt, and pour them into the empty half. Stir them in loose folds until barely set and still glossy, then slide them out onto the pork plate.
steps.tip: Undercook the eggs here since they finish in the hot pan later.

steps.text: Crank the heat to high and add the cabbage all at once. Let it sit against the metal without stirring so the cut edges blacken and blister, then toss and let it sit again until the leaves are wilted at the ribs but still snapping.
steps.tip: Real wok-style char is the difference between champuru and steamed cabbage.

steps.text: Return the pork and tofu to the pan, then pour in the soy sauce, mirin, sesame oil, and umami seasoning around the edges so they hiss and caramelize. Toss everything hard until the sauce clings and the pan is nearly dry.
steps.tip: Saucing down the hot sides toasts the soy instead of steaming the food.

steps.text: Kill the heat and fold the eggs and scallions back in with a few gentle turns so the egg stays in soft ribbons. Grind over plenty of black pepper.
Heat the jasmine rice according to the package while the pan rests. Serve the champuru over the rice and blizzard the whole thing with bonito flakes, which will curl and wave in the rising steam.
steps.tip: Add the bonito at the very last second so it moves at the table.

swap: No bonito flakes? Stir 1 tsp of instant dashi powder into the sauce and finish with toasted sesame seeds for texture.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat in a screaming-hot dry skillet rather than the microwave so the tofu and pork recrisp, and add fresh bonito on top.

title: Alsatian Coq au Riesling with Bacon and Mushrooms
blurb: Chicken simmered down in dry Riesling until the wine turns into a silky mustard-cream sauce studded with smoky lardons and deeply browned mushrooms.

ingredients.item: 4 slices Appleton Farms bacon, cut in lardons
6 oz wide egg noodles or spaetzle

steps.text: Set a heavy skillet over medium heat and render the lardons, stirring now and then, until they are crisp and have given up a pool of fat. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat in the pan.
steps.tip: Start them in a cold pan so they render rather than seize.

steps.text: Pat the thighs dry, season with salt and pepper, and sear them in the bacon fat over medium-high without moving them until the undersides are mahogany. Flip, brown briefly, and move them to a plate; they will finish in the sauce.
steps.tip: You want color, not doneness, at this stage.

steps.text: Add the mushrooms in one layer and leave them completely alone until they stop squeaking, release their water, and take on dark caramelized faces. Salt them only after they have browned.
steps.tip: Salting early pulls out water and stalls the browning.

steps.text: Drop the heat to medium, add the butter, shallots, and thyme, and cook until the shallots go soft and translucent. Sprinkle the flour over everything and stir until it disappears and smells faintly toasty.

Pour in the Riesling and scrape every browned scrap off the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble briskly until it has reduced by about half and the sharp alcohol smell has cooked off, and start your noodle water while you wait.
steps.tip: Taste the wine first; if you would not drink it, do not cook with it.

steps.text: Whisk in the cream and Dijon, then nestle the chicken back in along with its juices. Turn the heat to low and simmer gently, spooning sauce over the thighs, until the sauce coats a spoon and the chicken is cooked through.
steps.tip: Keep it under a boil so the cream stays smooth.

steps.text: Boil the noodles in well-salted water until just tender, drain them, and toss with a knob of butter and a pinch of pepper. Taste the sauce and adjust with salt and a little more mustard if it needs sharpening.

Spoon the noodles into warm shallow bowls, lay the chicken over them, and pour the sauce and mushrooms across the top. Scatter the crisp lardons and parsley over everything just before it goes to the table.
steps.tip: Adding the bacon at the end keeps it crunchy against the sauce.

swap: No Riesling? Any dry, aromatic white such as Pinot Gris or Sauvignon Blanc works; avoid anything oaky or sweet.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat the chicken and sauce covered over low heat with a splash of cream, and cook fresh noodles rather than reheating them.

title: Colombian Chicken Sancocho with Aji Picante
blurb: A golden, cumin-scented pot of fall-apart chicken, corn rounds, green plantain, and potatoes that thicken the broth themselves, served with a fierce green aji on the side.

ingredients.item: 4 lb bone-in skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks (Kirkwood)
2 green plantains, peeled and cut in thick chunks
3 ears corn, cut in 2-inch rounds (or 6 Season's Choice frozen cobbettes)
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut in large chunks
1 large bunch cilantro, stems and leaves separated

steps.text: Season the chicken hard with salt and pepper and pile it into a large stockpot with the onion, half the scallions, the garlic, one whole jalapeno, the cumin, the turmeric, and the cilantro stems. Cover with about 12 cups of cold water.
steps.tip: Starting in cold water draws more flavor out of the bones.

steps.text: Bring the pot to a boil over high heat, then immediately drop it to a bare simmer. Skim off the grey foam that rises in the first few minutes until the surface runs clear.
steps.tip: Skimming now is what gives sancocho its clean golden broth.

steps.text: Cover partially and simmer gently so the surface only trembles, until the chicken is tender enough that the meat pulls back from the bone ends. Taste the broth and season it well with salt.
steps.tip: A hard boil will cloud the broth and dry out the meat.

steps.text: While it simmers, make the aji: finely chop the cilantro leaves, the remaining scallions, and the second jalapeno, then stir them together with the juice of one lime, a splash of water, and a big pinch of salt. Let it sit so the flavors marry.
steps.tip: The aji should taste sharper and saltier than seems reasonable on its own.

steps.text: Add the plantain chunks to the pot and simmer uncovered until they are starting to soften but still hold together firmly at the center when pierced.
steps.tip: Green plantain releases starch that begins thickening the broth.

steps.text: Add the potatoes and corn rounds, pushing them under the liquid, and simmer until the potatoes are completely tender and a few edges have crumbled into the broth, thickening it to a light body.
steps.tip: Those disintegrating potato edges are the goal, not a mistake.

steps.text: Fish out the whole jalapeno and any loose bones, then pull the chicken pieces to a board if you want and slip the skin off. Return the meat to the pot in large pieces and taste the broth one last time for salt.
steps.tip: Leaving big bone-in pieces is traditional; boneless is easier for lunches.

steps.text: Let the pot rest off the heat so the flavors settle and the fat rises to skim if you like. Ladle into wide bowls with a piece of everything in each, and pass the aji and remaining lime wedges at the table.
steps.tip: Every bowl should get chicken, plantain, corn, and potato.

swap: No green plantains? Use 1 lb of frozen yuca chunks or an extra pound of potatoes, added at the same stage.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and the broth thickens considerably as the starch sets; loosen with water or broth when reheating and make a fresh batch of aji, which is best the day it is chopped.
